title: RBAC, Service Accounts and Kubeconfig

toc.title: A bug you will see: roleRef is immutable
Give a person a kubeconfig (CertificateSigningRequest flow)

html:
1How a request is checked

Every API request passes three gates, in order: authentication (who are you?), authorization (may you do this?), admission (is the object acceptable?). RBAC is the authorization gate. It is additive: there are only allow rules, no deny rules. No matching rule means "forbidden".

Who How Kubernetes knows them
A user (human) A client certificate (the certificate's CN is the user name, O is the group) or an external identity. Kubernetes has no User object.
A ServiceAccount A Kubernetes object; Pods use its token. Full name system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name>.
A group A label on the identity, for example the certificate's O field.

2The four objects

Object Scope Holds
Role one namespace permissions (rules)
ClusterRole whole cluster permissions; also for cluster-scoped resources (nodes, namespaces, PersistentVolumes) and non-resource URLs
RoleBinding one namespace who gets a Role or a ClusterRole inside that namespace
ClusterRoleBinding whole cluster who gets a ClusterRole everywhere

The pattern the exam loves: a ClusterRole bound with a RoleBinding grants those permissions only in that one namespace. The same ClusterRole bound with a ClusterRoleBinding grants it everywhere.

A rule has verbs (get list watch create update patch delete), resources (pods, deployments) and, for non-core resources, an API group (apps for Deployments; the core group is "").

3Fast commands (no YAML)

k -n dev create role pod-reader --verb=get,list,watch --resource=pods
k -n dev create rolebinding read-pods --role=pod-reader --user=jane
k create clusterrole cluster-auditor --verb=get,list --resource=nodes,namespaces
k create clusterrolebinding auditors-read --clusterrole=cluster-auditor --group=auditors
k -n ci create rolebinding x --clusterrole=deploy-manager --serviceaccount=ci:deployer
  • Resource with a group: --resource=deployments.apps.
  • Service account subject format for the flag: <namespace>:<name> (--serviceaccount=ci:deployer). A wrong namespace is a common bug.
  • Built-in ClusterRoles you can reuse: view (read most things in a namespace), edit, admin, cluster-admin.

4Test it: kubectl auth can-i

k auth can-i list pods -n dev --as jane                       # yes / no
k auth can-i list nodes --as someone --as-group auditors
k auth can-i create deployments -n ci --as system:serviceaccount:ci:deployer
k auth can-i --list -n dev --as jane                          # everything jane may do

Always finish an RBAC task with can-i: one "yes" and one "no" (a different namespace or verb) proves the scope.

5A bug you will see: roleRef is immutable

A RoleBinding's roleRef (which Role it points at) cannot be edited. If it names a Role that does not exist (a typo), kubectl edit fails; delete and recreate the binding. Check with k -n shop2 get rolebinding app-cm -o yaml. The other common mistakes: the subject's namespace is wrong, or a RoleBinding was used where a ClusterRoleBinding is needed (or the reverse).

6Service accounts and tokens

k -n ops create serviceaccount reporter
k -n ops create token reporter --duration=1h        # short-lived token, printed once
  • Every namespace has a default ServiceAccount. Pods use it unless spec.serviceAccountName says otherwise.
  • Modern clusters do not auto-create long-lived token Secrets; use create token.
  • Use the token as --token=$TOKEN against the API server to test what it can do.

7Give a person a kubeconfig (CertificateSigningRequest flow)

  1. Make a private key and a CSR whose subject is the user name: openssl req -new -key jane.key -subj "/CN=jane" -out jane.csr.
  2. Submit a CertificateSigningRequest with signerName: kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client, usages: [client auth], and request: set to the base64 of the CSR (single line: base64 -w0).
  3. Approve: k certificate approve jane. The signed certificate appears in .status.certificate (base64).
  4. Build the kubeconfig:
k config set-cluster kind-cka --server=$SERVER --certificate-authority=ca.crt --embed-certs=true --kubeconfig=jane.kubeconfig
k config set-credentials jane --client-certificate=jane.crt --client-key=jane.key --embed-certs=true --kubeconfig=jane.kubeconfig
k config set-context jane-ctx --cluster=kind-cka --user=jane --namespace=dev --kubeconfig=jane.kubeconfig
k config use-context jane-ctx --kubeconfig=jane.kubeconfig

Proof: k --kubeconfig jane.kubeconfig get pods works in dev and is forbidden elsewhere. A certificate alone gives no rights; the RoleBinding does.

Contexts in one line: a context = cluster + user + namespace. k config get-contexts, k config use-context <name>, k config view --minify shows the active one.

8Lab tasks

<!-- LABS: m02 -->

Lab 2.1: role binding

Domain: Architecture | Points: 5 | Time: about 5 minutes | Status: executed and validated on Kubernetes v1.37.0 (id m02-01-role-binding)

Context: kubectl config use-context kind-cka

In the namespace dev, create a Role pod-reader that allows the verbs get, list and watch on Pods only. Bind it with a RoleBinding named read-pods to the user jane. The user must not be able to delete Pods, and must not be able to read Pods in other namespaces.

Reference solution (try the task first; on the exam ssh <node> replaces the lab's docker exec):

kubectl -n dev create role pod-reader --verb=get,list,watch --resource=pods
kubectl -n dev create rolebinding read-pods --role=pod-reader --user=jane

Lab 2.2: sa clusterrole

Domain: Architecture | Points: 6 | Time: about 6 minutes | Status: executed and validated on Kubernetes v1.37.0 (id m02-02-sa-clusterrole)

Context: kubectl config use-context kind-cka

Create the namespace ci and a ServiceAccount deployer in it. Create a ClusterRole deploy-manager that allows get, list, create and update on deployments in the apps API group. Grant it to the ServiceAccount only inside the namespace ci (not cluster-wide).

Reference solution (try the task first; on the exam ssh <node> replaces the lab's docker exec):

kubectl create ns ci
kubectl -n ci create serviceaccount deployer
kubectl create clusterrole deploy-manager --verb=get,list,create,update --resource=deployments.apps
kubectl -n ci create rolebinding deploy-manager --clusterrole=deploy-manager --serviceaccount=ci:deployer

Lab 2.3: cluster wide read

Domain: Architecture | Points: 5 | Time: about 5 minutes | Status: executed and validated on Kubernetes v1.37.0 (id m02-03-cluster-wide-read)

Context: kubectl config use-context kind-cka

Members of the group auditors must be able to get and list Nodes and Namespaces across the whole cluster, and nothing else. Create a ClusterRole cluster-auditor and a ClusterRoleBinding auditors-read for the group.

Reference solution (try the task first; on the exam ssh <node> replaces the lab's docker exec):

kubectl create clusterrole cluster-auditor --verb=get,list --resource=nodes,namespaces
kubectl create clusterrolebinding auditors-read --clusterrole=cluster-auditor --group=auditors

Lab 2.4: fix rolebinding

Domain: Troubleshooting | Points: 6 | Time: about 6 minutes | Status: executed and validated on Kubernetes v1.37.0 (id m02-04-fix-rolebinding)

Context: kubectl config use-context kind-cka

In the namespace shop2, the ServiceAccount app cannot read ConfigMaps although a Role and a RoleBinding exist. Find the mistake and fix it so that app can get and list ConfigMaps in shop2 (and nothing outside that namespace). Keep the Role named cm-reader and the RoleBinding named app-cm. Hint: some fields of a RoleBinding cannot be edited; you may need to recreate it.

Reference solution (try the task first; on the exam ssh <node> replaces the lab's docker exec):

kubectl -n shop2 get rolebinding app-cm -o yaml | grep -A3 roleRef
kubectl -n shop2 delete rolebinding app-cm
kubectl -n shop2 create rolebinding app-cm --role=cm-reader --serviceaccount=shop2:app

Lab 2.5: user certificate

Domain: Architecture | Points: 8 | Time: about 10 minutes | Status: executed and validated on Kubernetes v1.37.0 (id m02-05-user-certificate)

Context: kubectl config use-context kind-cka

A new developer jane needs access. In the namespace dev, a Role and RoleBinding already let the user jane list Pods.

  1. Create a private key and a certificate signing request for jane and submit a CertificateSigningRequest object named jane (signer for API client certificates, usage client auth).
  2. Approve it and fetch the issued certificate.
  3. Create a kubeconfig file ~/answers/jane.kubeconfig with a user jane (embedded credentials), the cluster of the current context, and a context jane-ctx in the namespace dev that is the current context of that file. Prove it by running kubectl --kubeconfig ~/answers/jane.kubeconfig get pods.

Reference solution (try the task first; on the exam ssh <node> replaces the lab's docker exec):

cd ~/answers
openssl genrsa -out jane.key 2048 2>/dev/null
openssl req -new -key jane.key -subj "/CN=jane" -out jane.csr
kubectl apply -f - <<Y
apiVersion: certificates.k8s.io/v1
kind: CertificateSigningRequest
metadata: {name: jane}
spec:
  request: $(base64 -w0 < jane.csr)
  signerName: kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client
  usages: [client auth]
Y
kubectl certificate approve jane
for i in $(seq 1 20); do [ -n "$(kubectl get csr jane -o jsonpath='{.status.certificate}')" ] && break; sleep 1; done
kubectl get csr jane -o jsonpath='{.status.certificate}' | base64 -d > jane.crt
kubectl config view --raw --minify -o jsonpath='{.clusters[0].cluster.certificate-authority-data}' | base64 -d > ca.crt
SERVER=$(kubectl config view --minify -o jsonpath='{.clusters[0].cluster.server}')
kubectl config set-cluster kind-cka --server=$SERVER --certificate-authority=ca.crt --embed-certs=true --kubeconfig=jane.kubeconfig
kubectl config set-credentials jane --client-certificate=jane.crt --client-key=jane.key --embed-certs=true --kubeconfig=jane.kubeconfig
kubectl config set-context jane-ctx --cluster=kind-cka --user=jane --namespace=dev --kubeconfig=jane.kubeconfig
kubectl config use-context jane-ctx --kubeconfig=jane.kubeconfig
kubectl --kubeconfig jane.kubeconfig get pods

Lab 2.6: sa token

Domain: Architecture | Points: 6 | Time: about 6 minutes | Status: executed and validated on Kubernetes v1.37.0 (id m02-06-sa-token)

Context: kubectl config use-context kind-cka

Create the namespace ops and a ServiceAccount reporter in it. Give the ServiceAccount read-only access to everything inside ops only, using the built-in ClusterRole view. Then create a token for the ServiceAccount that is valid for one hour and save it to ~/answers/token.txt.

Reference solution (try the task first; on the exam ssh <node> replaces the lab's docker exec):

kubectl create ns ops
kubectl -n ops create serviceaccount reporter
kubectl -n ops create rolebinding reporter-view --clusterrole=view --serviceaccount=ops:reporter
kubectl -n ops create token reporter --duration=1h > ~/answers/token.txt

<!-- /LABS -->

9Recall questions

R1Does RBAC have deny rules?

Show the answer

No. It is purely additive; no matching allow means forbidden.

R2What is the effect of a ClusterRole bound with a RoleBinding?

Show the answer

The permissions apply only inside the RoleBinding's namespace.

R3Which API group do you put for Deployments in a Role rule?

Show the answer

apps (written deployments.apps in the --resource flag).

R4Which command shows everything a user may do in a namespace?

Show the answer

kubectl auth can-i --list -n <ns> --as <user>.

R5A RoleBinding points to a Role with a misspelled name. Can you fix it with kubectl edit?

Show the answer

No; roleRef is immutable. Delete and recreate the binding.

R6How do you get a one-hour token for a ServiceAccount?

Show the answer

kubectl create token <sa> --duration=1h -n <ns>.

R7What do the CN and O fields of a client certificate mean to Kubernetes?

Show the answer

CN is the user name, O is the group.

R8After the CSR is approved, where is the certificate?

Show the answer

In .status.certificate of the CertificateSigningRequest, base64 encoded.

Quick Reference Card

Topic Remember
Objects Role/RoleBinding (namespace), ClusterRole/ClusterRoleBinding (cluster)
Scope trick ClusterRole + RoleBinding = one namespace only
Create create role/clusterrole --verb --resource; create rolebinding/clusterrolebinding --user/--group/--serviceaccount ns:name
Verify auth can-i <verb> <resource> -n <ns> --as <user>
Immutable roleRef of a binding: delete and recreate
Tokens create token <sa> --duration=1h
Kubeconfig set-cluster, set-credentials, set-context, use-context with --kubeconfig
User cert CSR signer kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client, usage client auth, certificate approve
